I am a 55-year-old farmer in Quzhou County, and I have been farming this land for over thirty years. My family has about 16 mu of good flatland on the North China Plain. I did not go to high school, but I know this soil and this climate better than any book. Around here, the only system that makes sense is the wheat-maize double crop — plant winter wheat in early October, harvest it in early June, then immediately put in summer maize and harvest that by late September or early October. Everyone in my village does this. It is stable, the buyers come to us, and I have the machinery and irrigation wells to support it.

This year I will stick with what works. For the wheat, I will use an improved local variety like *shimai* or *liangxing*, sow about 30 jin per mu, and do rotary tillage before planting to break up the stubble and prepare a good seedbed. I will put down a basal compound fertilizer — about 100 kg per mu of the 18-22-5 blend — and topdress with 50 kg of urea in the spring when the wheat greens up. That gives the crop plenty of nitrogen to push for a high yield. I will irrigate three times: once at sowing or overwintering, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I will spray herbicide once and insecticide twice, and maybe a fungicide if the weather turns humid.

For the maize, I will plant a hybrid like *nongda372* or *denghai605* right after the wheat comes out. I use no-tillage for maize — there is no time to plow again in the hot summer, and the seed drills work fine through the wheat stubble. I will sow about one package of seed per mu and apply roughly 90 kg per mu of the high-nitrogen compound, the 28-6-6 blend. Maize needs less irrigation than wheat here; twice is usually enough, once at seedling stage and once at the big flare stage. I will spray herbicide once and insecticide twice to control armyworm and aphids.

I thought about planting cotton or vegetables on a small plot, but the prices are uncertain and I am getting older — managing the labor for picky crops is hard. I will put all 16 mu into the wheat-maize rotation. It is boring, but it pays the bills.
